note: Week 7 lessons: least privilege, governance and policy as code. Each lesson has a level (basics, intermediate or advanced) so the climb is visible.

lessons.title: Least privilege, roles, reviews and audit
lessons.inOneSentence: Least privilege means each person and system has only the access it needs, for only as long as it needs it, and governance is how a company keeps it that way over time.
lessons.youCanNow: Explain least privilege and just-in-time access, and state that 'explicit deny wins' is a rule of the specific policy engine in use, not a universal law.
lessons.whyItMattersToADesigner: Enterprise customers buy security products to prove control: who has admin rights, who approved them, when they were last checked. Designing roles, temporary access and access reviews is a senior-level problem that touches admins, managers, auditors and the buyer.
keyIdeas: You met least privilege on Day 4 and policies in Week 3. Now you design the systems that keep access small over months and years.
Admin roles split power: not every IT person should be able to delete the whole tailnet. Example roles: owner, admin, network admin, IT admin, billing, auditor (read-only).
Just-in-time (JIT) access: instead of permanent admin rights, people request access for a reason and a time (two hours for an incident), it is approved, and it expires on its own.
Access reviews: every quarter, managers confirm who should keep which access. Badly designed reviews turn into “approve all”, which is called rubber-stamping.

In cloud IAM, an identity-based policy is attached to a person or role (“what can I do?”); a resource-based policy is attached to a resource (“who can use me?”). An explicit deny always wins over any allow.
Audit logs prove it all: who granted what, who approved it and when it ended. Auditors ask for this evidence.
Break-glass accounts are emergency admin accounts kept locked away for when normal sign-in fails. They must be rare, alarmed and reviewed.

words.meaning: Only the access needed, only for as long as needed.
A named set of admin powers, such as network admin or auditor.
Temporary access requested for a reason and removed automatically.
A regular check of who should keep which access.
Approving everything in a review without really checking.
A policy attached to a resource that says who may use it.
A rule that blocks access and overrides any allow, in the policy engines Atlas covers — this precedence is a product/engine design choice, not a universal rule of every authorization system.
An emergency admin account used only when normal access fails.
No single person can complete a sensitive action alone.

steps.text: Read Tailscale user roles and list what each role can do.
Read Microsoft’s access reviews overview.
Read what Privileged Identity Management does.
Read Tailscale just-in-time access and compare it with PIM.
Read the AWS IAM best practices on least privilege and temporary credentials.
Skim IAM Access Analyzer to see how a tool finds unused or too-broad access.
Design on paper the review screen a manager sees for 12 people: what helps them decide well instead of approving everything?
Write three principles for designing least-privilege features.

lessons.skipOrSkim: Skip writing real IAM policies. Understand the patterns and the people involved.
checkYourself: What is just-in-time access, and why is it better than permanent admin rights?
Why do access reviews often fail, and what could design do about it?
How does an explicit deny interact with allows?
lookFor: Access is requested for a reason and a limited time, approved, and removed automatically. If an account is stolen, it usually has no standing admin rights to abuse, and every use is recorded.

Reviewers face long lists with little context, so they approve everything. Design can help with context (last used, risk level), smart defaults (suggest removing unused access) and smaller, focused reviews.
An explicit deny always wins. Even if another policy allows the action, the deny blocks it.

lessons.title: Compliance and policy as code, in plain words
lessons.inOneSentence: Compliance frameworks like SOC 2 and ISO 27001 ask companies to prove they control access and changes, and policy as code keeps those rules in files that are reviewed, tested and versioned like software.
lessons.youCanNow: Distinguish a SOC 2 report (an attestation) from ISO 27001 certification, and explain how policy-as-code differs from a full GitOps pipeline.
lessons.whyItMattersToADesigner: Compliance is why many companies buy security products, and policy as code is how technical teams want to manage them. A designer who can bridge the auditor’s need for evidence and the engineer’s need for git workflows can design features that sell and that people actually use.
keyIdeas: SOC 2 is a report from an independent auditor that a company’s controls work: who has access, how changes are approved, how incidents are handled. Customers ask suppliers for it before buying.

Type 1 checks that controls are designed well at one point in time; Type 2 checks they actually worked over months. SOC 2 itself is an attestation: an auditor's report on how well your controls work, not a pass/fail certification. ISO 27001 is different in kind: it is a certification against an international standard, issued after an accredited audit.
Auditors ask for evidence: screenshots, exports and logs that prove each control. Products that make evidence easy to export save customers weeks.
Policy as code: rules live in text files in git. Every change is a pull request that someone reviews, tests run automatically, and you can see history and roll back.
GitOps means git is the source of truth: when a change is merged, a pipeline applies it automatically. Tailscale supports this for its policy file.

Open Policy Agent (OPA) and Cedar (Week 3) are both policy-as-code engines, but they are not interchangeable: each has its own policy language and evaluation model, so a policy written for one cannot simply be dropped into the other.
The design challenge: some admins edit in the console, some in git. Products must keep both consistent and show clearly which one is in charge.

words.meaning: An independent audit report on a company’s security controls.
An international standard for managing information security.
A practice or rule that reduces risk, such as requiring approval for changes.
Proof that a control works: logs, exports, screenshots.
Keeping rules in versioned files that are reviewed and tested like software.
A proposed change in git that others review before it is merged.
Using git as the source of truth, with changes applied automatically after merge.
Open Policy Agent: a widely used policy-as-code engine.

steps.text: Read the first sections of the plain-language SOC 2 guide.
Skim the official SOC page to see who defines SOC 2.
Read the Open Policy Agent introduction and one example.
Re-read Tailscale just-in-time access and note what evidence it leaves behind.
Skim the SC-300 study guide headings to see which governance skills enterprises expect admins to have.
Pick one control, such as “access changes are reviewed and approved”, and list the evidence an auditor would ask for and where it would come from in Tailscale.
Sketch how a product could show “this policy is managed in git” in its console, and what an admin can and cannot do there.

lessons.skipOrSkim: Skip the full SOC 2 criteria and ISO clauses. Know what they are for and what evidence looks like.
checkYourself: What is the difference between SOC 2 Type 1 and Type 2?
What are three benefits of policy as code?
Why must a product show clearly whether a policy is managed in git or in the console?
lookFor: Type 1 checks that controls are well designed at one moment. Type 2 checks that they actually operated over a period, usually several months.
Every change is reviewed in a pull request, tests run before it goes live, and there is a full history with easy rollback.
Otherwise an admin edits in the console and the next git sync silently overwrites the change, or the two drift apart. Clear ownership prevents confusion and lost changes.

lessons.title: Exercise 16: an access policy managed in git
lessons.inOneSentence: You will move your Exercise 6 policy into a git repository, change it through a pull request with tests, and roll it back, as a platform team would.
lessons.youCanNow: Propose an access-policy change as a pull request and explain what review and automated tests it should pass before merging.
lessons.whyItMattersToADesigner: This is how many technical customers of Tailscale and Tigera really work. Doing it yourself shows you where the console and git experiences meet, and gives you a design insight for case study 1: policy changes need review, preview and safe rollback.
keyIdeas: Your policy file becomes a file in a GitHub repository. A GitHub Action tests and applies it to the tailnet when a change is merged.
The workflow: create a branch, edit the policy, open a pull request, tests run, someone reviews, merge, the change goes live.
Your ACL tests from Exercise 6 now run in the pull request: a failing test blocks the merge.
Rollback is just reverting the commit. Notice how much safer this feels than editing live in a console.
As a designer, notice what the pull request does not show: who will gain or lose access in human terms. That gap is a design idea.

words.meaning: A project folder tracked by git, often on GitHub.
A separate line of changes in git.
GitHub’s system for running automatic steps, such as tests, on changes.
Accepting a pull request into the main version.
Undoing a change by adding a commit that reverses it.

steps.text: Read GitOps for Tailscale.
Set up GitOps with GitHub Actions for your test tailnet, following the guide.
Make a change through a pull request: add a group and a rule, with tests. Make one test fail on purpose, then fix it.
Merge, check the change in the console, then revert it and check again.
Write notes: what the pull request showed, what it did not, and a sketch of a “who gains or loses access” summary for reviewers.

lessons.skipOrSkim: Skip Terraform and other tools unless you already use them. One tool, done end to end, is enough.
checkYourself: What does a test in the pull request protect against?
What does a reviewer of a policy pull request need to see that a text diff does not show?
lookFor: It stops a change that breaks an expected access promise from being merged, so mistakes are caught before they reach real people and systems.
The effect in human terms: who will gain or lose access to what, how risky the change is, and which tests cover it. A text diff shows only changed lines.

lessons.title: Case study 1: concepts, flows and prototype
lessons.inOneSentence: You will design a policy editor that shows admins who will be able to reach what before they save, using everything from Weeks 3 to 7.
lessons.youCanNow: Develop a concept, user flow and prototype for an access-policy editor.
lessons.whyItMattersToADesigner: This is the core design of your first case study. It must show senior skills: several concepts compared, clear reasoning from evidence, and a prototype that handles a complex technical subject in a way admins can trust.
keyIdeas: Start from your problem statement and research log. Every design choice should link to evidence.

Generate at least three concepts before choosing: for example (1) a live “effect preview” beside the editor, (2) a “who can reach X?” query tool, (3) a change summary like the pull request idea from Exercise 16.
Use progressive disclosure: show the plain-language effect first (“12 people in Sales will lose access to the wiki”), with the rule details one click away.
Design for both worlds: admins who edit in the console and teams who use git. Your preview can appear in both places.
Include the hard states: a change that locks everyone out, a conflict with git, a test that fails, and an empty policy for a new tailnet.
Build a clickable prototype of the main flow: edit a rule, see the effect, fix a problem, save with confidence.

words.meaning: An early design direction, explored before committing.
Showing the result of a change before it is saved.
An unusual situation the design must still handle.
A clickable model of a design, used for testing.
The reasons behind design decisions.

steps.text: Read about progressive disclosure.
Read the guidelines for complex applications and use them as a checklist.
Sketch three concepts on paper and compare them against your problem statement and metrics.
Choose one concept and design the main flow in Figma, with the key edge cases.
Link the frames into a clickable prototype for testing tomorrow.

lessons.skipOrSkim: Do not polish visual style. Spend time on the effect preview and the hard states.
checkYourself: Why compare three concepts before choosing one?
How does your design help an admin trust a change before saving it?
lookFor: It avoids falling in love with the first idea, shows hiring managers your process, and often produces a better solution that combines the strengths of several concepts.
For example by showing in plain words who gains or loses access, flagging risky changes, running tests before saving and making rollback easy.

lessons.title: Case study 1: test and improve
lessons.inOneSentence: You will test your policy editor prototype with two people, ideally admins or engineers, and change it based on what you see.
lessons.youCanNow: Test the access-policy-editor prototype with a participant and make one evidence-based improvement.
lessons.whyItMattersToADesigner: Testing turns a nice idea into evidence. Even two sessions with the right people reveal the biggest problems, and a case study that shows “what I learned and changed” is far stronger than one that shows only final screens.
keyIdeas: Give people a realistic task, not a tour: “Contractors should no longer reach the wiki. Make that change and check nothing else breaks.”
Ask them to think aloud. Do not help or explain; note where they hesitate, misread or are surprised.
Watch especially for trust: do they believe the effect preview? Would they save the change?
After both sessions, sort observations into “must fix”, “should fix” and “later”. Fix the must-fix issues in the prototype today.
Record before and after for the case study: the problem you saw, the evidence and the change you made.

words.meaning: Watching people try to complete tasks with a design.
Asking participants to say what they think as they work.
A realistic goal given to a participant in a test.
An observation from testing, backed by what you saw.
Changing a design based on what you learned, then testing again.

steps.text: Read usability testing 101.
Write two task scenarios and a short script.
Run two 25-minute sessions (remote is fine) and take notes.
Sort the findings and fix the most important ones in the prototype.
Write down the three most important findings with before and after.

lessons.skipOrSkim: If you cannot find admins, test with engineers or designers, and say so honestly in the case study.
checkYourself: Why give a task rather than a tour in a usability test?
What was your most important finding, and what did you change?
lookFor: A task shows whether people can actually do the job with the design. A tour only tells them what you meant, and they will agree politely.
A good answer names a real observation (what the person did or said), why it mattered, and the specific change to the design.

lessons.title: Case study 1 draft: write it up and share
lessons.inOneSentence: You will write the first full draft of case study 1: problem, research, concepts, design, testing and what changed.
lessons.youCanNow: Write an honest, structured first draft of the access-policy case study.
lessons.whyItMattersToADesigner: This is your first complete portfolio piece in the new domain. A clear, honest story with real evidence is what hiring managers at companies like Tailscale look for, and early feedback from a practitioner makes it much stronger.
keyIdeas: Structure: the problem and why it matters, your role and constraints, research and evidence, concepts and the choice, the design, testing and changes, outcome and next steps.
Lead with the problem and the result in the first screen of the page; busy readers decide in 30 seconds.
Show technical understanding plainly: one diagram of how access rules work, with your design on top.
Label honestly: this is a self-initiated concept, not shipped work. State who you tested with.
Ask one practitioner for feedback with two specific questions, for example “Is the problem real for you?” and “Would you trust this preview?”

words.meaning: Work you chose and did yourself, not for a client or employer.
What changed because of the work, or what you expect to change.
Comments from others used to improve your work.

steps.text: Write the full draft (900–1,400 words) with the key frames.
Make the opening: problem, your role, the result, in three short paragraphs and one image.
Send it to one practitioner with two specific questions.
Post a short version or save it in your portfolio folder.
List what you will polish in Week 9.

lessons.skipOrSkim: Do not aim for perfect. A complete draft with feedback is the goal this week.
checkYourself: What does a reader learn in the first 30 seconds of your case study?
How do you label this work honestly?
lookFor: The problem, why it matters, what you did and the result or key insight. A good opening makes the reader want to keep scrolling.
As a self-initiated concept project, stating who you researched and tested with and what is assumed. Honesty builds trust with hiring managers.
